text: An EC2 key pair is a standard public/private key pair used for authentication instead of a password. AWS keeps the public key and installs it into the instance's authorized-keys file the moment you launch pointing at it. The private key is handed back exactly once, in the API response — AWS never retains a copy, so losing it means replacing the key yourself or launching a fresh instance.

create-key-pair generates the pair and writes the private key material to a local .pem file. chmod 400 matters on Linux and macOS, because SSH refuses to use a private key file that other users on your machine could read. There is no step where AWS asks you to confirm you saved it — once the response is gone, so is your only copy.

A security group is a stateful, instance-level firewall that works entirely on allow rules — there's no deny rule to write, because anything not explicitly allowed is denied by default. A brand-new group blocks all inbound traffic until you add a rule like this one, which opens port 22 only from a specific CIDR range instead of the entire internet. Outbound traffic, by contrast, is allowed by default until you lock it down.

Stateful means the response to an already-allowed request is automatically permitted — allow inbound port 22, and the reply traffic going back out just works, with no matching outbound rule required. That's what separates a security group from the stateless network ACLs covered later. With the public key installed on the instance and the security group open to your address, connecting is one command: -i names the private key file, ec2-user is the default login for Amazon Linux AMIs (ubuntu on Ubuntu AMIs), and the address is the instance's public IP.

If that SSH command fails, the cause is almost always the security group not allowing your current IP on port 22, or the wrong username for the AMI — not some deeper mystery. That closes out EC2 for this chapter. Next up: AWS storage, starting with S3 buckets, objects, and the storage classes that control what you pay to keep data around.
